{"code": "import pandas as pd

# Load the data
df = pd.read_csv('/home/musel/Github/research_agent/data/sales.csv')

# Step 1: Remove refunded orders — they are not conversions
completed_only = df[df['status'] == 'completed']

# Step 2: Parse revenue as float, removing commas
completed_only['revenue'] = completed_only['revenue'].str.replace(',', '').astype(float)

# Step 3: Remove QA orders with revenue 999999.99
# These are not real orders and would distort mean revenue
real_orders = completed_only[completed_only['revenue'] != 999999.99]

# Step 4: Check for missing age — -1 is sentinel for missing
# We will not use age in the analysis, but note it
print(f"Number of missing age entries: {(real_orders['customer_age'] == -1).sum()}")

# Step 5: Verify the premises
# Premise 1: Campaign was run on email — yes, channel is email
# Premise 2: Not randomly assigned — yes, email was targeted at loyal customers
# Premise 3: Targeted loyal customers — yes, as per documentation
# Premise 4: Conversion rate = proportion of converted = 1

# Now, compute conversion rate by channel
# But note: raw comparison is confounded because email was targeted at loyal customers
# So we must stratify by customer_segment

# Cross-tabulate channel vs customer_segment
cross_tab = pd.crosstab(real_orders['channel'], real_orders['customer_segment'])
print("Cross-tabulation of channel vs customer_segment:")
print(cross_tab)

# Summary: email has more loyal and returning customers, paid_search has more new
# So if we compare raw conversion rates, email will look better — but not because of the campaign
# We need to adjust for customer segment

# Compute conversion rate within each customer_segment
conversion_by_segment = real_orders.groupby(['channel', 'customer_segment'])['converted'].mean().reset_index()
print("Conversion rate by channel and segment:")
print(conversion_by_segment)"}
